title: SYSK Selects: How Sign Language Works
summary: Saturday "SYSK Selects" rerun of the 2014 episode on how sign language works. Josh and Chuck introduce the episode, then cover the history of deaf education and the deaf community, the Martha's Vineyard Sign Language case, Thomas Hopkins Gallaudet and Laurent Clerc and the American School for the Deaf, Gallaudet University, American Sign Language (ASL) grammar and linguistics (phonology, morphology, topic-comment syntax, tense, space, facial markers, directionalizing, fingerspelling and indexing), a fake sign interpreter at Nelson Mandela's memorial, sign language etiquette, signed exact English, Pidgin Signed English, International Sign, baby sign language, and a listener email asking for an episode on HIV. The original episode title is not stated in the rerun intro beyond the title itself.

segments.title: Selects intro
segments.summary: Josh introduces this Saturday Selects episode, picked from February 2014, and says it was fascinating to learn about sign language.

segments.title: Opening banter and article overview
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the HowStuffWorks article by Jonathan Strickland, noting there are hundreds of sign languages and that regional dialects exist, and that they will focus mainly on American Sign Language.

segments.title: Historical mistreatment of deaf people
segments.summary: The hosts describe historical mistreatment of deaf people, including restrictions in Torah temple rituals, Greek limits on education, and St. Augustine's view. Education of deaf people began in the Renaissance, and deaf communities developed their own sign languages.

segments.title: Martha's Vineyard Sign Language
segments.summary: Hereditary deafness on Martha's Vineyard led to a community where many people used Martha's Vineyard Sign Language, practiced from about 1700 until the last deaf resident died in 1952. Oliver Sacks reportedly interviewed elders who switched between speech and sign.

segments.title: Gallaudet and the American School for the Deaf
segments.summary: Thomas Hopkins Gallaudet went to France to learn teaching methods, worked with Roch-Ambroise Cucurron Sicard and student Laurent Clerc, and founded the American School for the Deaf in Hartford, Connecticut in 1817. This blended French and existing American sign language, which is why ASL is partly rooted in French Sign Language. Gallaudet University in D.C. was also founded.
topics: French Sign Language roots of ASL

segments.title: Gallaudet University and campus controversy
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Gallaudet University's football team and its student body, which includes some hearing students. They mention a mid-2000s controversy over a president raised to speak rather than sign.

segments.title: ASL linguistics: phonology, morphology and grammar
segments.summary: ASL has its own grammar, syntax and phonology. Phonology in sign is a discrete set of hand shapes and movements that can be altered, and morphology is how signs are formed. ASL drops English syntax, and signs can be modified in size, speed and direction, such as eat, food, and give.

segments.title: Iconic signs, facial expression and space
segments.summary: Signs can be iconic, such as the sign for deer and moose. Facial expression and body language are part of the grammar. Signing near or far from the body shows recency or distance in time, and tense is marked at the start of a sentence and changed when needed.

segments.title: Fake sign interpreter at Mandela memorial
segments.summary: A man who was a fraudulent sign interpreter at Nelson Mandela's memorial service made up gibberish. The hosts say he was hired at a lower rate and that he reportedly suffers from schizophrenia. Deaf viewers noticed his lack of facial expression.

segments.title: Fingerspelling, indexing, and new signs
segments.summary: Fingerspelling is an alphabet used for names and specific concepts. Indexing points to a location to represent someone absent. New signs are created, like fiscal cliff, and people debate whether ASL should evolve. Interpreters in Washington, D.C. are discussed.

segments.title: Sign language etiquette
segments.summary: Etiquette includes waiting for the signer to finish and looking back before responding, not interrupting, and watching facial expressions when the signer addresses an imaginary person. Walking between two signers is considered acceptable, though going around is preferred.

segments.title: Signed Exact English, Pidgin Signed English, and International Sign
segments.summary: Signed Exact English follows English syntax and is slower, and educators often prefer it. Pidgin Signed English sits between it and ASL. International Sign, from the World Federation of the Deaf, is unified but far from codified.

segments.title: Baby sign language
segments.summary: Parents teach hearing babies signs for needs like milk or mommy starting around six months. Researchers reported these babies had better speech and language, and parents pair signs with spoken words.

segments.title: Listener mail: HIV episode request
segments.summary: A listener named Jesse from San Francisco shares a story about a friend's reaction to his HIV status and asks for an episode on how HIV works. The hosts agree to consider it.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts remind listeners how to contact the show and where to find transcripts and more episodes.
